posts.title: China has about 15 million passenger cars with NOA as driver assistance adoption expands
posts.summary:
About 61 million passenger cars in China had L2 driver assistance features as of August, including about 15 million equipped with NOA.
For details, please visit CnEVPost (cnev.co).
bullets: As of August 2026, China's passenger vehicle fleet includes approximately 15 million cars equipped with Navigation on Autopilot (NOA) capabilities.
NOA-enabled vehicles now represent 25% of the total 61 million passenger cars in China featuring Level 2 driver assistance systems.
The Chinese government is actively standardizing connected-vehicle technology, with over 400 standards currently under development across intelligent transportation and communications sectors.
Vehicle connectivity is scaling rapidly, with 16 million passenger cars now equipped with 5G terminals and 2 million utilizing C-V2X technology.

posts.title: VW targets China's electric sedan market with Xpeng-powered ID. UNYX 09
posts.summary:
Volkswagen Anhui has launched the ID. UNYX 09 with a limited-time starting price of 169,900 yuan ($25,290).
For details, please visit CnEVPost (cnev.co).
bullets: Volkswagen Anhui has launched the ID. UNYX 09 electric sedan, the second model developed in partnership with Xpeng, featuring a starting price of 169,900 yuan.
The vehicle is equipped with CATL's 5C fast-charging battery cells, enabling a range increase of 250 km from just 5 minutes of charging.
The sedan integrates Xpeng's Turing AI chip, providing 750 TOPS of computing power to support advanced driver-assistance features like urban NOA and VLA-based autonomous driving.
The launch signals Volkswagen's aggressive push into China's large electric sedan segment, utilizing Xpeng's software stack to compete with domestic EV manufacturers.

posts.title: CATL confirms Qilin Battery powers Nio Firefly with 560 km range
posts.summary:
CATL confirms Firefly uses its Qilin Battery, with the 60-kWh version offering a CLTC range of 560 km.
For details, please visit CnEVPost (cnev.co).
bullets: Nio's Firefly brand has introduced a 60-kWh battery option using CATL's Qilin technology, extending the vehicle's CLTC range to 560 km.
The new NCM-cell battery maintains the same dimensions as the entry-level 42-kWh LFP battery supplied by Sunwoda, allowing for seamless upgrades via Nio's battery swap network.
Existing Firefly owners can perform a permanent battery upgrade for 17,000 yuan, while BaaS subscribers face a higher monthly rental fee of 599 yuan for the larger pack.
The integration of standardized module designs across different battery capacities highlights Nio's strategy to leverage its battery-as-a-service model for long-term vehicle lifecycle management.

posts.title: Why Physical AI Is So Hard To Engineer
posts.summary:
Integrating sensors, compute, and actuators into autonomous systems adds new challenges for chip design.
The post Why Physical AI Is So Hard To Engineer appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Physical AI represents a shift from generative text/code models to systems that must perceive, decide, and act autonomously within unstructured physical environments.
The transition to physical AI introduces critical safety requirements, where a 1% error rate can have life-or-death consequences, necessitating new design methodologies and simulation tools.

Industry experts emphasize that physical AI is as much an imaging and sensor-fusion challenge as it is a compute challenge, requiring tighter integration between sensing, inference, and real-time control.

posts.title: How far can we push computing?
posts.summary: MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here. On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s…
bullets: The tech industry is currently relying on 'brute force' scaling, with hyperscalers projected to spend over $700 billion on infrastructure in 2026, doubling the record set in 2025.
Traditional performance gains driven by Moore’s Law and Dennard’s Law are stalling, forcing a transition from easy miniaturization to the physical limits of atomic-scale computing.

The massive capital expenditure on data centers is outpacing the capacity of the electrical grid, highlighting a growing tension between the demand for AI compute and the physical constraints of energy and hardware density.
